title: Rare Bernini painting discovered in Vienna museum storeroom ahead of major exhibition.
summary: A new painting by Renaissance master Gian Lorenzo Bernini has been discovered and will be unveiled in December at Vienna’s Kunsthistorisches Museum, according to The Art Newspaper . The painting, titled Portrait of an Old Man , a nearly life-size depiction of an elderly man with disheveled white hair and an intense, direct gaze, had been attributed to an anonymous 17th-century Roman artist and was moved into storage in 1989 for lack of a firm attribution. Bernini, primarily known as a sculptor and architect, never signed his paintings, and fewer than 20 are widely accepted as authentic. The portrait entered the museum‘s collection in 1920 as a work attributed to Philippe de Champaigne , bequeathed by Viennese collector Richard Lieben, who had purchased it in 1900; nothing is known of its earlier provenance. Over the following century it was reattributed multiple times, to an anonymous Italian painter, to the French artists de Champaigne or Jean Jouvenet , to the Flemish artists Jacob Ferdinand Voet or Erasmus Quellinus the Younger , and more recently to Bernini‘s collaborator Baciccio . Kunsthistorisches Museum curator Gudrun Swoboda now argues the work is Bernini‘s, dating it to around 1670 based on the sitter‘s clothing, collar, and hairstyle, which reflect Roman fashions of the period. She points to the painting‘s sense of space and anatomical precision, along with parallels to Bernini‘s bust of Louis XIV, particularly around the mouth. Swoboda describes the paint handling in the face as sculptural, “building up and modelling a face in clay” with short, bristled brushstrokes, and sees further stylistic echoes in a Bernini self-portrait drawing in the U.K.’s Royal Collection dated 1675–80. She believes the finely painted head and collar are Bernini’s work, while the more weakly rendered black garment and shoulder were completed by another hand, possibly one of his sons—a division a recent scientific examination has corroborated. Swoboda speculates the sitter may be Mario Chigi, a brother of Pope Alexander VII and Bernini’s most important late patron. The attribution is contentious in part because Bernini is generally thought to have stopped painting around 1650, two decades before the Vienna work’s proposed date. Of the roughly 16 paintings currently accepted as his, only one dates from after 1640. If confirmed, the new attribution would substantially revise the timeline of Bernini‘s painting career. Portrait of an Old Man will anchor “Bernini: Painter and Sculptor” at Vienna‘s Palais Lobkowitz, running December 2nd through April 4th, 2027, alongside loans including the Uffizi’s Bernini self-portrait and the Royal Collection drawing.

title: 5 New Restaurants in New York Where the Art Is as Impressive as the Food
summary: The worlds of food and art are colliding in New York City. In the past year, a handful of restaurants have opened with impressive culinary offerings that parallel the artwork inside. While some are associated with art organizations such as Sotheby’s and the New Museum , others get their creative flair from the owners’ taste. The topic is becoming the talk of the town, including in Artnet’ s recent podcast, The Art Angle , which features Annie Armstrong, food and culture writer for Caper Media. And it’s not just the art world that is creating buzz. Reviews in major outlets are also driving diners to these new artful haunts. Whether you’re refueling after a museum visit or fancy your appetizers with a side of art, here are five of the best new restaurants in New York with art collections that are guaranteed to satisfy as much as the fare. Oriana 174 Mott Street What to see: Tribeca gallerygoers, your new go-to restaurant is here. A short walk away to Nolita is Oriana, the latest spot from fine-dining institution Eleven Madison Park alumni chef Andy Quinn and sommelier Cedric Nicaise, who together also launched Noortwyck in the West Village in 2022. Dark browns fill Oriana’s stunning space designed by local architecture firm Modellus Novus, and are warmed by a wood-fired grill. Artworks from the restaurant’s financier and building owner Kevin Ryan’s collection fill the walls, including pieces by Rashid Johnson , Alteronce Gumby , and Ming Smith . But the stunner is a site-specific mural by Tunji Adeniyi-Jones featuring the British artist’s characteristic vibrant palette with swirls of lush flora and fauna that draw from his Yoruba heritage. The rich blues and orange hues span 25 feet in the multi-panel work, gracing the large dining room with thrilling energy. “We wanted the interiors of Oriana to reflect the deep artistic history and spirit of downtown New York by filling the walls with visual artists who inspire us as well as our guests,” said Christopher Omachi, who advised on the restaurant’s collection. “We knew Adeniyi-Jones’s paintings wouldn’t fade into the background—they bring a sense of depth, movement, and life to the restaurant, beckoning people in from the street and inviting conversation amongst guests.” What to eat: Adeniyi-Jones’s mural sets a spirited tone that is matched by the energy of the room. The menu centers around live-fire and open-grill dishes, with chic diners indulging in rich dishes like perfectly cooked hanger steak and smoky, roasted vegetables, as well as lighter fare like briny oysters and silky tuna crudo. A highlight is the wood-fired salmon over a smoked butter sauce that pairs perfectly with maitake mushrooms. Each dish is packed with flavors and fresh ingredients like ramps and basil that add brightness to both the plate and the palate. Oberon, New Museum 235 Bowery What to see: With the sleek design by architectural firm OMA and partner Shohei Shigematsu, it’s no surprise that Oberon inside the New Museum is stylistically impressive. Bathed in warm browns, including cork booths encircling the walls and a low, curved ceiling, Oberon feels like the inside of a cave or a coffee bean, a contrast to the metal surfaces throughout the museum. Above the bar is an agentic AI digital installation by Ian Cheng that responds to the activity of the room. Diners can also play a game of virtual chess while sitting at the sculptural bar top, which was designed by artist Minjae Kim , who also created some of the cozy tables and resin-dipped fiberglass artworks floating over the booths. After dinner, guests receive chocolates with poems by Laurie Anderson . “While we're an independent business with an independent entrance, we're still in and of the museum and its community. We wanted the entire space to reflect the community, which is by and for artists, and to feel creative rather than be a gallery,” said Henry Rich, managing partner of Oberon. “Everything is meant to be integrated into the experience, not too distracting, and with an artist’s sensibility more than the discrete pieces you might see in the museum. This way people can tune into the art or just enjoy the experience.” What to eat: Oberon has refreshingly reasonable prices and an approachable menu of seasonal modern American fare, with staples like a burger and fettuccine, as well as dorade bursting with flavorful romesco and summer squash. A highlight was a generous serving of prawns with a zippy blend of salsa negra, jalapeño, and cilantro, which pairs perfectly with the bright dressing of coconut yuzu on the watercress salad. Oberon’s audience isn’t just museumgoers. While the New Museum closes at 6 p.m., the restaurant stays open until 1 a.m., an enticing invitation to have a glass of wine while playing AI chess late into the night. Bar Chimera 550 Madison Avenue What to see: Inside legendary architect Philip Johnson ’s postmodern masterpiece (the former AT&T building), restaurateur Simon Kim has assembled a spectacle to match the building’s scale. Bar Chimera is the latest addition to Kim’s Gracious Hospitality portfolio, which includes Michelin-starred Korean steakhouse COTE. Bar Chimera is three bars in one: martini, whiskey, and wine. Designed by the Rockwell Group, the room is carefully divided into distinct zones, from the gleaming chrome martini counter to the wood-paneled whiskey library and convivial wine bar. London-based artist Martin Creed ’s neon signs, commissioned by ARTLINE, hover on the walls. “We felt that Creed’s ability to bring people together aligned seamlessly with the values of 550 Madison: hospitality, community, and positivity,” said Ji Park Kwak and Rosa Suehyun Kim, the founders and directors of public art consultancy ARTLINE. “In striving to realize an artistically meaningful and innovative art program that stands apart from the typical large corporate midtown landscape, we were drawn to the sophisticated playfulness and embracing openness of Martin’s work.” The artworks’ glowing text, like a yellow sign that reads “Don’t Worry,” are lighthearted statements visible from the street and throughout the grandiose space. “We wanted Bar Chimera to feel like a sort of zen resting spot within the intensity of Midtown,” added Simon Kim. “The inspiration for the space came in part from ancient cities like Rome, where you might find a fountain just outside a busy merchant area, giving people a place to pause and rest after a bustling day.” What to eat: The drinks program is a suitably extensive highlight. The martini is the star, with ice made from filtered and re-mineralized water and a choice of garnishes ranging from pickled onions to blue-cheese-stuffed olives. The menu here is a combination of New York brasserie classics and elevated bar snacks with Korean American flourishes. A perfect option for indecisive diners or people who like to try multiple dishes is the brilliant preset menu with seven small appetizers like red snapper crudo and wagyu bresaola with melon to accompany your choice of an entree. The burger comes with peppercorn mustard and a brioche bun (with a side of fries, of course), yet there’s no need for any additional accouterments. Its flavors are remarkably complex, making it a strong contender for one of New York’s favorite arguments: the best burger in the city. Zoli Amant, 312 Maujer Street, Brooklyn What to see: There’s nothing unusual about a fish tank in a restaurant, but the tank at Zoli will catch you by surprise. With three large rectangular aquariums, the marine habitats are part of a work by artist Pierre Huyghe . The piece was commissioned by Amant founder and collector Lonti Ebers: The avant-garde artwork matches the atmosphere the adjacent art center is known for. Unlike the tanks some restaurants have with creatures like lobsters that might soon become dishes, Huyghe’s are intentionally off-putting with alien-like crabs and GloFish (genetically modified to emit artificial hues) in murky water. The aquatic triptych is inspired by nearby Newtown Creek, one of the most polluted estuaries in New York City. The water levels in the tanks rise and fall as if responding to an unknown tide, and the glass occasionally switches from opaque to transparent, adding a cinematic effect. What to eat: Zoli’s seafood-forward menu changes frequently, but the small plates are light and flavorful, making for a great shared experience and return visits. A surprising star of the menu is the “Olney salad,” whose ingredients change often, but are an assortment of fresh herbs and lettuces dressed in incredibly fine oil and vinegar. Each dish is packed with bold and unexpected flavors, like the mussel dressing on the Romano beans with sungolds. Marcel, Sotheby’s 945 Madison Avenue What to see: An endeavor between auction house Sotheby’s and the design firm Roman and Williams, Marcel is the French restaurant inside Sotheby’s headquarters, which opened last November . The Marcel Breuer–designed Brutalist building provides a dramatic setting, with soaring ceilings, large windows, and views of the sculpture garden. Having two creative leaders at the helm, it’s no surprise that Marcel is expertly outfitted, from the tableware to the lighting fixtures in cast bronze and cast glass by Roman and Williams that complement Breuer’s signature circular designs overhead. And, of course, there’s the art on offer from Sotheby’s. While an energetic Willem de Kooning painting and an abstract John Chamberlain sculpture might accompany your next meal, the selection will continue to change. The dining room, vitrines, lobby, stairwell, and garden terrace are packed with blue-chip fare, which at the time of publication also included works by Isamu Noguchi , Pierre-Auguste Renoir , Andy Warhol , Louise Nevelson , and others. What to eat: Diners can rub elbows with collectors, tourists, and salespeople alike. But not all is business and power lunches at Marcel, as the food entices as much as the art. The high prices preclude a casual outing, but for a special occasion there’s a reliable selection of French-leaning continental cuisine and brasserie fare like confit duck, foie gras, and onion soup.

title: Swedish rapper Yung Lean to present first major art exhibition in Stockholm.
summary: Jonatan Leandoer Håstad, the Stockholm-born musician better known as Yung Lean, will present his first visual art exhibition, “Collected Works 2016–2026,” at Torsgatan 22 in Stockholm from September 25th through October 11th. The show brings together a decade of paintings, collages, works on paper, sculpture, and dioramas—most never before exhibited—alongside a site-specific installation and a new narrative short film that Håstad executive produced and stars in. Rather than a standard gallery hang, the works are staged in different environments such as a salon, a television room, and a screening room. Håstad, who is self-taught, organized the exhibition himself rather than working with an outside curator. It follows a recent live painting installation with Adidas Originals during Paris Fashion Week earlier this year, and several Instagram teasers released by the artist. “Ever since I can remember I dreamed of colors,” he said in a statement. “I’ve made wooden sculptures and drawings and paintings since I was a kid. Just like my songs, the work is made through stream of consciousness. I go where the hand takes me.” Following the Stockholm run, a selection of works, primarily sculptures, will go to an international online auction in partnership with Bukowskis. The exhibition arrives amid a broader run of musicians and actors staging their own visual art shows. Last summer, Ed Sheeran opened “ Cosmic Carpark Paintings ” at HENI Gallery in London, a collection of Jackson Pollock -influenced drip works made in a disused carpark and sold alongside prints for £900 ($1,224) each, with half the proceeds going to the Ed Sheeran Foundation. Sheeran was direct about the reference point and about his own standing as an artist: “It’s mostly just splashing colors on canvases, think Jackson Pollock... I am by no means ’an artist,’ but I do love making art.” Academy Award-winning actor Adrien Brody similarly opened “Made in America” at Eden Gallery in New York last year, his first show of new work in nearly a decade . The show featured large-scale mixed-media paintings and a sound installation of his own composition. Its opening also followed a $425,000 sale of a collage by Brody at the amfAR Cannes gala. In Håstad’s case, his surreal imagery has run alongside his music since he emerged as the face of the Swedish rap collective Sad Boys and the cloud rap movement that rose to popularity in the early 2010s. “My paintings mean nothing and also everything,” said the rapper of the exhibition “Here they are.”

title: Why Women Bodybuilders Are Everywhere in Contemporary Art
summary: In Keerthana Kunnath’s photo series “Not What You Saw,” groups of brawny bodybuilders gaze potently into the lens as they bend and flex their muscles. But these depictions aren’t what you might expect of the physically demanding sport. Soaked in the golden southern Indian sun, wrapped in ornately embellished fabric, glittering jewelry, and flowers, these bodybuilders are powerful young women from Kerala. Bodybuilding is an art form as well as a sport, celebrating shape and presentation as well as brute strength. These muscular celebrations, in art history, have usually been of men: from Frederic Leighton ’s mighty and undeniably phallic 1877 sculpture An Athlete Wrestling with a Python to Michaelangelo ’s towering 16th-century marble masterpiece David . Today, the gym bro aesthetic is a key part of the “manosphere,” as it’s often called, with male politicians such as Pete Hegseth showing themselves working out on social media to prove their masculinity. In this cultural climate, contemporary artists are looking to women bodybuilders to reimagine gender and beauty stereotypes, allowing their mighty female protagonists to be variously brave, monstrous, beautiful, and always in control. Rather than portraying women as meek and mild, these artists capture the glamour and sexuality of their women bodybuilder subjects, as well as their physical potency. Pin Up from the Magazine Lady Face Man Body, No. 3, 2011 Cassils Human Rights Campaign Benefit Auction It’s not the first time that the gender implications of bodybuilding have been the subject of contemporary art. In Cassils ’s 2011 project CUTS , the Canadian performance artist used bodybuilding techniques and steroids to put on 23 pounds of muscle in 23 weeks, resulting in a photo series that depicts the transgender artist as a masculine, yet glamorous, figure. Kunnath likewise decided to focus on bodybuilding to explore the gendered standards of her childhood. She started her career in fashion photography in London. When she began photographing bodybuilders in southern India in 2024, she wanted to do something different: confront traditional expectations of how a woman should look and behave. “Growing up, there were always so many ideas around what a woman should be and how much space she was allowed to take up,” the photographer told Artsy ahead of her first solo museum exhibition opening at Foam Fotografiemuseum in Amsterdam on September 18th. “I was drawn to the women themselves; their individuality, confidence, and the fact that they had chosen a path so different from what we typically see women pursue from the region.” Kiss of Fire, 2022 Ana Benaroya Two Palms Her subjects are photographed against a southern Indian landscape, dressed in a blend of traditional outfits from the region to create a juxtaposition with their built physiques. The images are also inspired by posters for vintage Malayalam films, where actresses would be shown as coquettish and pliable. “I wanted to borrow some of that visual language but turn it on its head,” she said. “I wanted the women to feel glamorous and powerful, but without taking away from their strength.” Glamour is also a key part of the 2022 series “Core” by London-based photographer Celia Croft and art director Kate Kidney Bishop. In one image, a muscular woman stretches a pair of diamanté-encrusted bikini bottoms across her firmly toned glutes. Another photo is reminiscent of a devotional painting as it shows a woman gazing up into the light, her eyelids covered in icy blue eyeshadow, as her long acrylic nails stroke her clavicle. Across the series, these women are physically powerful and enticingly glamorous. “The whole bodybuilding industry is about muscle, strength, power—and these women are redefining femininity and gender and finding a new space within that,” the pair said in an interview. In this sense, women bodybuilders capture high femme sexuality as well as the physical strength usually associated with men. American painter Ana Benaroya revels in these two distinct aesthetics in her paintings of physically commanding women. Inspired by Michelangelo’s depictions of the body and contemporary photographs of bodybuilders, her female figures are flamboyant and frenzied, depicted in a palette of acid green, bright purple, electric blue, and hot pink. Their undulating muscles are enormous, creating the appearance of brawny goddesses. They also have flowing hair, enormous breasts, and talon-like nails. In Spirit Colossal (2025), for example, two women are painted in vibrant red and blue, flexing against a natural backdrop of wildflowers and glittering night sky. “I love creating a balance between perceived opposites within my paintings,” the artist told Artsy. “I never want the women in my work to seem like one thing.” Her works are also inspired by art historical depictions of women, where their sexuality is foremost. “Women’s bodies as objects of desire is something that is almost impossible to escape, but I am interested in harnessing that to my own end,” she said. “Yes, they can be ripped but they can also be voluptuous and do their hair and nails….They are powerful and monstrous, alluring and beautiful.” Bodybuilder Beauty, 2023 Elsa Rouy Larsen Warner Spirit Colossal, 2025 Ana Benaroya KOSAKU KANECHIKA That ambiguity is also on view in the work of British artist Elsa Rouy . Her painted bodies merge together, variously muscular, bony, and bendy. In her 2023 painting Bodybuilder Beauty , a bald figure proudly holds their arms above their head. Their biceps ripple, ribcage flares, and breasts are pulled up near their chin. “There’s an ambiguity and strength with the bodybuilder physique that I found interesting and wanted to explore,” Rouy told Artsy. “There’s a ferocity to it. I’m constantly trying to look into the push and pull of the body at breaking points and moments of intensity.” For Bodybuilder Beauty , she was also inspired by a drawing by Jusepe de Ribera , who was known for his sinewy subjects. “Translating the contorted male body into one of a bold and confronting ambiguous figure was fun to do and a way of expressing my own ideas about alternate femininity.” These vibrant depictions of physically extreme women create a new vision for preconceived notions of gendered behavior and appearance. As Kunnath told Artsy about the people in her photographs, “There is something really beautiful about seeing these women inhabit their bodies on their own terms, without trying to make themselves smaller or more conventionally feminine.”

title: Why This Ghanaian Collector Is Committed to Buying African Artworks that Feel Like Home
summary: For Dr. Myma Belo-Osagie, collecting art began with a simple goal: to fill her bare dorm room in law school. While at Harvard University, the Ghanaian lawyer, collector, and arts patron wanted something to make her space feel less anonymous. Then she encountered a print of a portrait of an African man by Peter Paul Rubens . “Something in his expression stayed with me long after I walked past it,” she recalled. “I think it was the first time an image really spoke to me and how I was feeling at the time and caused me to want to have it with me rather than simply admire it from afar.” That encounter sparked an impulse to live with art that has remained at the center of Belo-Osagie’s art-buying ethos. Over the years, she has built a collection of more than 400 works spanning painting, ceramics, sculpture, tapestry, and quilts. She places particular emphasis on artists from Nigeria, Ghana, and across the African continent, including Larry Otoo , Ehinomen Okoeki , and Ndidi Dike. From private pleasure to responsibility “I have always bought what I like and what I find interesting—not necessarily because a piece is ‘valuable,’ whatever that means,” she told Artsy. In the early years, that meant buying from artists who were young, relatively unknown, and sometimes struggling to make a living. While that instinct remains, her understanding of what support entails has evolved. A collection of this scale, she has come to recognize, “comes with certain obligations: documentation that fully acknowledges the artists, proper care, and thinking about what happens to the works after me.” Collecting, she said, has evolved “from simply being a private pleasure to becoming something closer to a responsibility to our society.” That sense of responsibility is particularly pronounced in Belo-Osagie’s approach to African art. “I am drawn to work that captures African life and identity—scenes and items that reference the way we live, the way we see beauty, the things we use on a daily basis, the things that feel like ‘home’ to me,” she explained. Her interests are also material. A work does not have to be conventionally beautiful or immediately legible to hold her attention. She is intrigued by objects that make her wonder how they were made and why an artist chose a particular material. She points to a sculpture by Nigerian artist Jacob Jari constructed almost entirely from cornstalks, which she acquired because she found it fascinating “that something so ordinary and ‘basic’ could be used to create art.” Her tastes, meanwhile, remain fluid. “My favorite [artwork] tends to shift depending on the day of the week and my mood,” she said. One work she repeatedly returns to is Moyo Ogundipe’s Three Lagos Socialites (2007), a densely layered painting depicting a familiar social scene in the Nigerian city. Belo-Osagie is captivated by its detail and by the way it takes a subject explored by other artists and renders it with distinctive complexity. Building support for artists beyond the collection As her collecting practice has expanded, so has her engagement with philanthropy. For several years, Belo-Osagie was part of an NGO that encouraged Nigerian companies like banks and corporations to buy and display Nigerian art. In 2025, her four children launched the Myma Art Prize to celebrate her 70th birthday. The prize rewards early- to mid-career artists from Ghana or Nigeria with $5,000, a funded residency, an exhibition, and professional development support—reflecting Belo-Osagie’s belief that financial support alone is not enough to sustain an artist’s career. “I began my collecting of African art at a time when many talented artists could barely survive on art sales alone,” Belo-Osagie explained. “But money was never really the entire issue.” Early promise can bring attention, she noted, but once the spotlight moves on, artists still need professional support to continue developing their practices. The experience of the prize’s first winner, Omolola Coker , has affirmed how beneficial the multifaceted approach can be. During Coker’s residency with Nosona in Benin City, Nigeria, she requested to extend her stay. For Belo-Osagie, it suggested that Coker remained open to being “stretched and refined.” During the residency, Coker has expanded beyond her primary practice of painting and experimented with other media, including bronze casting. Reimagining a history of patronage The prize’s format reflects a broader conception of patronage rooted in African history. “Historically we have thought of patronage as wealthy families, individuals, or institutions supporting art and artists by commissioning works and funding artists,” Belo-Osagie explained. “In pre-colonial times, the Asantehene [the Asante kingdom in Ghana] and the Oba of Benin [the Benin kingdom in Nigeria] and their respective palaces were largely responsible for supporting the artists and gold and bronze casters.” Their support led to the creation of the renowned gold weights in the Asante kingdom and the world-famous Benin Bronzes. This form of patronage, Belo-Osagie explained, was significantly reduced during the slave trade and colonization. With this model in mind, Belo-Osagie views her role as a collector with a keen understanding of the impact her support has on individual artists, as well as on the broader industry. “Ultimately collectors help to create legacy and stability for the art world,” she said. “Certainly for Africa I feel one of the major responsibilities is to help develop an art ecosystem that works for the way we, as Africans, want to live today and furthermore, one that provides better understanding and context for not just the intrinsic value of works of African art but also for the economic value art brings to the creative economy and the GDP of our countries.” Collecting as preservation For Belo-Osagie, supporting artists also holds a deeper mission to remind future generations of what was lost in the arts due to colonialism and the slave trade. “I see part of this responsibility as further rebuilding and reviving the awareness amongst a younger generation of the incredible talent, skill, and creativity Africa had in the arts, and restoring confidence in our ability to continue to create and innovate in this space,” she said. Collecting, in this sense, becomes an act not only of preservation, but restoration.

title: Anna Weyant paints Marc Jacobs for "Vanity Fair" cover.
summary: Anna Weyant has painted designer Marc Jacobs for the cover of Vanity Fair' s Style 2026 issue, for the cover story ”Marc Jacobs Cannot Tell a Lie.” Published August 18th, the story coincides with Jacobs's sale of his namesake label, Marc Jacobs International, which is estimated at $850 million. Weyant’s portrait depicted Jacobs in Chanel tweed, teal flower earrings, and his hair held back with silver salon clips, rendered in Weyant's Old Master –inspired style against a dark, painterly background. The portrait appears on the cover alongside a line by the poet Walt Whitman, which reads, ”From this hour I ordain myself loos'd of limits and imaginary lines.” This is the second time Jacobs has commissioned Weyant to put her own subjects into his world. In December 2024, as Vogue 's first external guest editor, Jacobs tapped Weyant to paint model Kaia Gerber in a Marc Jacobs Fall 2024 dress, for one of two alternate covers of the magazine's December issue, telling Vogue at the time, ”I love Anna's women, and I love the idea of Kaia seen by Anna.” Loose Screw, 2022 Anna Weyant The BlackWood Gallery The two collaborated again more recently when Weyant transformed Manhattan's Academy Mansion into a life-size, walk-through dollhouse during New York Fashion Week, populated with models dressed in Jacobs's dollhouse-themed collection, an installation presented with the bank Capital One and membership club The Cultivist that drew guests including actress Phoebe Tonkin and Jacobs himself. Meanwhile, for the 2026 Met Gala , Weyant wore a pink lace-trim organza slip dress from the Marc Jacobs Spring 2025 runway. Weyant, 31, is known for close, faintly unsettling scenes of girlhood rendered in a Dutch Old Masters–inflected technique, her sfumato shading giving figures a porcelain delicacy shadowed by unease. Represented by Gagosian since 2022, she hit her auction record that year when Falling Woman (2020) sold for $1.6 million at Sotheby's, eight times its high estimate. Vanity Fair has tapped artists for its covers in the past. Most recently, British artist Issy Wood painted a portrait of Charli XCX for Vanity Fair' s November 2025 art-issue cover.

title: Major collection of cat-related art and collectibles heads to Bonhams auction this fall.
summary: This fall, Bonhams will present the Sandy Lerner Cat Collection, a two-part sale of one of the most significant private collections of cat-related decorative arts, books, and collectibles ever assembled. The first part of the auction will be hosted live at Bonhams New York on September 30th. The second runs online September 22nd through October 1st. The auctions draw from the Ayrshire Farm estate of businesswoman, philanthropist, and feline aficionado Sandy Lerner. Bonhams will also present two additional auctions from Lerner’s estate, including furniture, paintings, and decorative arts from her Georgian Revival Virginia residence, held in Massachusetts, later in the fall. Lerner, who co-founded tech company Cisco Systems and later founded the cosmetics brand Urban Decay, has spent more than three decades building the cat collection. She chronicled her collecting journey in the 2017 book Caticons: 4,000 Years of Art Imitating Cats . The collecting habit began, by her own account, during a period when she was “forced to be catless” because her then-husband was allergic; she has said her only criteria for acquisitions were “(1) is it a cat, and (2) do I like it?” “These are objects I have personally chosen,” Lerner said in a statement. “They need to be rehomed, now, to others who will care for, cherish, and respect them as icons of the human achievement and—in the case of the caticons—affection that created them.” The Sandy Lerner Cat Collection Part I will feature 66 lots spanning centuries and media. Highlights include Léonard Tsuguharu Foujita ’s Chat et Chaton (1934) estimated at $30,000–$50,000; Diego Giacometti ’s Tête de Chat (circa 1970) estimated at $20,000–$30,000; and Henri Matisse ’s Visages et grenades (circa 1952) estimated at $10,000–$15,000. Other artists represented in the sale include Rembrandt Bugatti , Édouard Manet , Théophile Alexandre Steinlen , Fernando Botero , and Henriëtte Ronner-Knip . The sale also includes feline-inspired jewelry from Tiffany & Co. and Boucheron, along with Asian works of art such as a Qing dynasty jade cat-form snuff bottle estimated at $30,000–$40,000. Beyond cats, furniture, decorative arts, and paintings from Lerner’s collection will be featured in Ayrshire Farm: The Sandy Lerner Collection Part I, a live auction in Massachusetts on October 28th. Animal-themed works reflecting Lerner’s broader affection for wildlife appear prominently in that sale as well, including Walter Hunt ’s Feeding Time , estimated at $25,000–$35,000. An online companion sale runs October 18th through 29th.

title: American painter Mary Heilmann dies at 86.
summary: Mary Heilmann , whose insouciant, wobbly-edged abstractions upended the precision of Minimalism and Modernist geometry, died Friday at a hospital in Riverhead, New York. Her studio confirmed the cause was complications from a recent fall. Born Mary Ann Heilmann in San Francisco on January 3, 1940, she grew up between the city and Los Angeles in an Irish Catholic family. Her father, a civil engineer, died when she was 13; her mother, a nurse, once warned that a life as an artist would mean she’d “starve in a garret.” “In my mind, I thought, ’Yes!’” Heilmann recalled in an interview with Bomb magazine in 1999 . “That’s exactly what I wanted.” She studied English literature at UC Santa Barbara, where she met the ceramicist Ron Nagle and took her first pottery classes, later pursuing ceramics and sculpture at San Francisco State University and at Berkeley under Peter Voulkos . After earning her master’s degree, she moved to New York in 1968, falling in with a downtown circle at the renowned Max’s Kansas City nightclub that included Robert Smithson , Carl Andre , Dan Graham , and Richard Serra , a friend from high school. Heilmann’s sculptural ambitions stalled when she was excluded from the Whitney Museum of American Art ’s landmark 1969 show “Anti-Illusion: Procedures/Materials,” of whose 22 artists only two were women (Dia Art Foundation would showcase Heilmann’s sculptures in the context of better-known male peers with an influential 2017 exhibition ). She turned to painting instead, calling it, in her 1999 memoir The All Night Movie , “a rebellious move” into “the much-maligned practice.” Her early paintings, including Little 9 x 9 (1973), made by wiping away pigment with her fingers, reworked the rectilinear grids of artists like Piet Mondrian and Sol LeWitt with off-kilter lines and dripping, high-key color. In 1978, after the deaths of the art dealer Norman E. Fisher and the artist Gordon Matta-Clark , she painted The End , a yellow rectangle marred by splashes of blood-red, calling it “a requiem” for those she had loved and lost. The following year, she painted Save the Last Dance for Me , an image of shrinking pink rectangles on black, a work she would consider the breakthrough that established her mature style. By the early 1980s, she felt shut out of the downtown scene: “My clothes were out of style. I’d lost my timing.” The spare paintings that followed, including Rosebud (1983) and Sea Wall (1986), are now considered among her finest. Gallerist Pat Hearn gave Heilmann the first of seven solo shows at her New York gallery beginning in 1986; Swiss powerhouse Hauser & Wirth began representing Heilmann in the late 1990s. Describing her process in 1987, she said, “When I make a painting, I’m like a kid stacking blocks; I push the shapes around in my mind, I count.” She also became known for boxy plywood chairs with webbed polypropylene seats, begun in 2002. Dozens of her chairs were installed on the Whitney Museum of American Art ’s outdoor terrace in 2015 to help inaugurate its Meatpacking District building, and reappeared inside a decade later in “Long Line,“ a show named for a 2020 painting enlarged across the gallery’s walls. Heilmann only received widespread recognition late in her career. Her first American museum retrospective, “ Mary Heilmann: To Be Someone ,” opened in 2007, when she was 67, at the Orange County Museum of Art in Newport Beach, California. The exhibition then travelled to the Contemporary Arts Museum Houston, the Wexner Center for the Arts in Columbus, Ohio, and New York’s New Museum . Later shows included the San Francisco Art Institute, Kunstmuseum Bonn, and London’s Whitechapel Gallery . “I have always worked from a sort of underdog position and got a lot of energy from that,” she told Whitehot Magazine in 2007. “So being ’top dog,’ now, is a little bit unsettling—I don’t exactly have the moves for that... but I’m gettin’ ’em!” “The big boys just totally marginalized Mary because she was turning the whole construction of hard-edged geometry inside out,” the artist Marilyn Minter told the New York Times in 2008. Writing in Bomb magazine in 1999, Ross Bleckner said her paintings “contain a joy so contagious one smiles upon seeing them.” Heilmann herself was matter-of-fact about the sentiment running through her work: “I like to get at deep sentiments through sentimentality,” she said. She never married and had no children; she is survived by two nieces and a nephew. Asked how she developed ideas for her paintings, she offered a characteristically unadorned answer: “I mostly just think. A lot of it is daydreaming. A lot of it is sitting.”

title: Why Norway’s “Trillion Dollar Man” Loves Buying Unexpected Art
summary: Even CEOs get summer jobs. Nicolai Tangen, the head of Norway’s sovereign wealth fund—the public fortune created by the country’s vast oil deposits—has been nicknamed Norway’s “Trillion Dollar Man.” Yet this summer he has been a tour guide in his hometown of Kristiansand on Norway’s southern coast. Tangen has been showing people around Kunstsilo, the £50 million (about $67.8 million) project that turned a monumental Brutalist grain silo on the town’s dock into a showcase for his collection of Nordic modern art . He gifted the whole package to his town in the summer of 2024. Although the part-private, part-public funding model for its running costs was hugely controversial, the institution has become a phenomenon: Time magazine hailed it as one of the “World’s Greatest Places.” Behind the unlikely summer gig is one of the more consequential collecting projects in recent Nordic art history. Over two decades, Tangen has assembled thousands of works with the explicit aim of challenging established national canons, championing artists who have fallen from fashion, and filling gaps in the historical record. Now, with the collection installed in a major public museum, his private taste has acquired unusual institutional—and market—power. Tangen’s collection ranges from works by internationally renowned figures from the region, such as the late Danish CoBrA artist Asger Jorn , through to lesser-known characters, including the Swedish figurative painter Ola Billgren , whose works offer a hazy blend of Hitchcock and Hockney . Highlights can be enjoyed in the current exhibition “Pictures from a New World: Stories from the Tangen Collection.” On his summer break from his state job, Tangen—an improbably energetic 60-year-old—has been guiding public groups through the galleries in a canary-yellow Kunstsilo-branded gilet, a microphone clipped to its lapel. His delivery is folksy and engaging. “You see where you keep people’s attention, when you get it completely silent, and when they want to move on,” he noted, talking to Artsy following one of the tours. He had them laughing, especially when introducing the more outré pictures. Any jokes fall flat? “Sure,” he acknowledged. “I wasn’t very saucy this time.” The word collector can mean “so many things,” observed Tangen. “I think it starts by defining your area of interest, and what it is that speaks to you as a person. So first you have to define and frame, and then the work starts.” He is not interested in acquiring works by “the flavor of the year…I know exactly who they are, these artists who everyone else is buying. We’re not buying any of it. We’re doing the opposite: we’re buying stuff that is out of favor. And, frankly, we define art history. This is a scholastic collection.” Tangen’s use of “we” is deliberate. Throughout his collecting adventure, he has worked with specialists in each of the Nordic countries. “I really don’t like ‘I,’” he said. “It would be very dishonest to pretend I’ve done all this by myself. One person cannot build this; it’s too comprehensive,” he explained. “You’d have to fly around like a madman.” His key advisor has been the art historian Steinar Gjessing, who also helped form the collection of the late Norwegian business tycoon Stein Erik Hagen (from which Tangen has acquired some 400 works). The motivation behind the Tangen Collection has always been “to find gaps in and alternatives to the national canon,” noted Gjessing. “To demonstrate that there are many stories. Many layers. Many voices.” Tangen grew up in Kristiansand in the 1970s; his early interest in art came from his art historian mother. Later, he built the successful AKO Capital hedge fund in London, before taking the helm at the Norwegian oil fund in 2020. His artistic interests remained throughout: in 2003, he took a two-year sabbatical to study for an MA at the Courtauld Institute of Art in London. The first artist to catch Tangen’s eye was Johannes Rian, the mid-century Norwegian painter, whose colorful figurative works echoed those of his teacher Axel Revold and, in turn, Revold’s teacher Henri Matisse . And then came the German-born Norwegian artist Rolf Nesch , on whom Tangen wrote his Courtauld thesis. “He came in quite early in my thinking. It’s partly the composition of the work; it’s the colours; it’s the technique. The whole thing that makes it powerful on the wall. I didn’t know about him.” He began with Norwegian works before panning out to Swedish, Danish, and, finally, Finnish art. There was a financial advantage to his strategy. “When I started, art from the 1950s wasn’t very sought after, so you could just scoop up the most incredible things.” Tangen’s activities have single-handedly driven prices up for the artists featured in the collection. “Now it’s hyper fashionable.” Tangen’s tastes have changed—finessed—over the years. “In the beginning it was a bit decorative and simple, and then it became complicated pretty quickly. My heart is closest to abstract art. I think abstraction is modernism and the way you disentangle color and form.” His collection is particularly strong in works that fragment landscapes and interiors: Anna-Eva Bergman ’s monumental rock forms, Tove Jansson ’s café interiors. Tangen’s other great interest is literature. He recently interviewed Susan Cain, author of Quiet: The Power of Introverts in a World that Can’t Stop Talking, on his In Good Company podcast (a platform for business leaders and contemporary thinkers). Cain told Tangen that his 10-year-old self would reflect his true character. “I think that is so interesting because I was an introvert, just read books all the time. And I think I have gone back to that,” he said. Next year Kunstsilo and U.K. literature festival Hay will collaborate on a new literature festival in Kristiansand. The event will have an international focus, Tangen noted, adding that contemporary Norwegian fiction has got stuck in a rut of “gloomy nothingness.” Although the Tangen collection is not without its fair share of melancholy pictures. “We have a lot of it,” he said. “That could fill another exhibition. You could call it: ‘Sad as Hell.’” Collecting has taken him out of boardrooms and—tentatively—into studios. “I’ve never been very close to the artists whose work I collect. I think proximity can easily bias you,” he said. “Business people tend to be more uniform and alike, in my experience. Artists often carry different struggles, and their art becomes a way of expressing and working through them. I enjoy spending time with both business people and artists. I think it lets me use two different sides of myself.” Today, Tangen only buys works for Kunstsilo. What he hangs at home are the “leftovers” from earlier collecting days. “I haven’t bought anything privately since 2015,” he said. “Happiness is in the mind; happiness is not about a painting or something you have on the wall. I never miss anything. I like change. When we’re done here next week, I’m not going to miss the summer; autumn is coming up.”

title: Works by Marina Abramović and Martin Creed featured in Balloon Museum New York’s inaugural show.
summary: The Balloon Museum opened its first permanent location on August 7th at the Tin Building at South Street Seaport in Lower Manhattan. Known for its inflatable structures and immersive sensory spaces, the Balloon Museum has previously held temporary exhibitions in Paris and London, drawing millions of visitors. The Balloon Museum inaugurates its New York home with “Daydream—Air Becomes Art,” an exhibition with new work by Marina Abramović alongside pieces by Martin Creed , Karina Smigla-Bobinski , Alex Schweder , Thom Kubli, Boris Acket, Hyperstudio, and Rub Kandy, among others. Abramović’s Snowy/Windy/Spring on Planet Z marks her first work to use air as a primary medium, following an artistic career built on duration, endurance, and viewer participation. “I’ve never done anything like this in my life. But if you give me an assignment then I’ll try to see what I can do with it,” Abramović said of her commission for the museum, in an interview with the Guardian . Meanwhile, Creed’s Work No. 3883: Half the air in a given space fills part of a gallery with blue balloons, while Smigla-Bobinski’s ADA consists of a large floating sphere studded with charcoal that visitors push around the room, leaving marks across the walls as it drifts. Outside the museum, Kandy’s oversized, googly-eyed GINJOS have already begun appearing around the Seaport. “Balloon Museum was founded on the idea that air and inflatables could become a powerful contemporary language,” said Balloon Museum president and Lux Entertainment CEO Roberto Fantauzzi in a statement. “Establishing a permanent home in New York is an extraordinary milestone for our organization and a reflection of how far this vision has grown.” Tickets for “Daydream” are available at peak and off-peak rates, with child pricing and family bundles offered.

title: Play based on Francis Bacon’s relationship with George Dyer opens at Edinburgh Fringe Festival.
summary: Three Figures and Portrait, 1975 Francis Bacon Tate Liverpool Buggers , a new play tracing the volatile relationship between painter Francis Bacon and his lover and muse George Dyer, has premiered at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival, running at Pleasance Courtyard through August 30th. Written by and starring Alistair Hall as Bacon, with Peter Clements as Dyer, the production is the first to receive research access from the Estate of Francis Bacon, which allowed Hall to draw on personal documents, letters, and artifacts in developing the script. Structured as a triptych, echoing the artwork format Bacon used throughout his career , the play unfolds across three fractured time periods, rather than following a linear timeline. It opens with the pair’s first night together in 1963, when Bacon, already an internationally acclaimed painter, became consumed by Dyer, a charismatic East End petty criminal roughly half his age. As Bacon painted him more than any other subject , Dyer grew increasingly dependent on the world of fame and excess that Bacon offered him while struggling with alcoholism and a deteriorating sense of self. The relationship, marked by sadomasochistic power dynamics and contained violence, is directed by Alice Wordsworth with movement direction by Ken Nakajima and set design by Rosie Elnile. The play builds toward Dyer’s death in a Paris hotel room in 1971, from an overdose of barbiturates and alcohol, two days before the opening of Bacon’s retrospective at the Grand Palais . Bacon had been consumed by preparations for the show in Paris, leaving Dyer behind at the hotel. Dyer’s death, and Bacon’s guilt over it, would recur throughout the artist’s subsequent work, including in his “ Black Triptychs ” of the early 1970s. In a five-star review of the production for the Guardian , critic Arifa Akbar called it a “phenomenal flesh and blood portrait,” praising Hall and Clements’s performances as charged with “real intensity” amid “a visceral psychodrama of contained violence and sadness.” She singled out the play’s wordless opening sequence and its closing device—reading aloud the titles and dates of the many paintings Francis Bacon made of Dyer—as particularly effective in conveying the emotional weight of their decade-long relationship. Buggers runs through August 30th, with no performances on August 17th and 24th.

title: 9 Artists on the Books They’re Reading This Summer
summary: Summer brings its own rhythm to the art world. Many galleries turn to group exhibitions, international shows draw audiences to scenic seasonal destinations, and the art fair calendar quiets until September. For artists, that change of pace can also create something increasingly rare: sustained time to read for pleasure. Books, of course, are often inseparable from an artist’s practice. A memoir can offer a new way of thinking about a life; an unexpected case study can open up a line of research; a collection of essays can sharpen, complicate, or unsettle an idea already taking shape in the studio. Reading may be especially pleasurable in summer—on a beach, in a park, during a quiet stretch at home—but it is rarely only a diversion. Books can become sources, provocations, and points of departure, sometimes feeding directly into new bodies of work or exhibitions. With that in mind, Artsy asked a group of artists with busy months ahead what they are reading this summer. As they prepare for solo and group exhibitions, biennial and fair participations, they share the books currently sitting on their desks, nightstands, and daybeds. Ali Banisadr B. Tehran, 1976. Lives and works in New York. Reading: Frances Yates, The Art of Memory , 1966 “Books often become companions in my studio. This summer, I’ve been returning to Frances Yates’s The Art of Memory . I’ve long admired Yates’s writing and have read her other books over the years, but this one has taken on a particular resonance while preparing for my upcoming exhibitions, ‘Talisman’ at Thaddaeus Ropac Paris and my exhibition at the Musée Gustave Moreau , also in Paris, opening this September. “What fascinates me is her idea that memory images become ‘inner talismans’—images that are internalized and continue to shape how we see and understand the world. I’ve realized this is also how I read: I read, reflect, return to passages repeatedly, and then let them rest. During that process, ideas become images, connecting with memory, dreams, music, and lived experience until they eventually reappear in my paintings. “Perhaps this is why I paint—to better understand the strange life of images, how they are remembered, transformed, and rediscovered across time. I am spending most of my time this summer in the Forest, Hudson Valley, New York.” Dominic Chambers B. St. Louis, Missouri, 1993. Lives and works in New Haven, Connecticut Reading: Anne Truitt , Daybook: The Journal of an Artist , 1982 “I’ve been reading Daybook: The Journal of an Artist , by sculptor Anne Truitt . This book has been more of a thought companion than a source of inspiration that directly influences my work. “More precisely, this book is about the life of an artist—her meditations on form and color, her doubts and wit, and the pendulum between motherhood and solitude, and so on. Body Shimmer (Bright Thoughts #1), 2026 Dominic Chambers Lehmann Maupin “Reading about the lives of other artists always fills me with courage. It is difficult to make work against the backdrop of our dismal political, social, and economic background. Reading Daybook has given me a reprieve in spiritual conversation and, when played aloud as an audiobook, has been a stimulating voice to produce work with.” Hew Locke B. Edinburgh, 1959. Lives and works in London. Reading: V.S. Naipaul, Miguel Street , 1959 “The book I plan to reread is Miguel Street by V.S. Naipaul. There is a darkness in this book, alleviated by an equally dark humor—my mother read this to my brother and sister and me as a bedtime story, which in retrospect was quite an unusual, almost adult choice of book. I have read it several times but not for a number of years, so I am looking forward to picking it up again. Kings & Queens 3, 2025 Hew Locke Cristea Roberts Gallery “As I get older, I see more and more in the book. It is a pleasurable read and is, in essence, a collection of beautifully written short stories about a boy growing up in Port of Spain in Trinidad during World War II, and in each chapter Naipaul brings to life one of the street's inhabitants in a short story. They are tragic—disturbing often—but also funny, such as Man Man, who lives on the street and declares himself the new Messiah. “The characters remind me of people I saw around me when I was growing up in Georgetown, neighboring Guyana. And this book has always been at the back of my mind for my whole career, for example in a new series of paintings of Knights Errant that I have been making recently.” Paula Siebra B. Fortaleza, Brazil, 1998. Lives and works in Fortaleza. Reading: Soetsu Yanagi, The Beauty of Everyday Things , 2018 “ The Beauty of Everyday Things by Soetsu Yanagi captivates me with the sincerity and delicacy of the author, who is an artist and collector of Japanese folk art. “The book is a collection of essays in which the author analyzes various types of traditional items, highlighting the sophistication in these everyday objects—bowls, small plates, and fabrics for kimonos made from banana leaves—especially when crafted by ordinary people. “He lavishes praise on the simplicity of these sturdy objects made to last, with little or no ornamentation, which we sometimes carry with us throughout our entire lives. I found it an essential read for reflecting on how a people’s identity is tied to a few motifs that recur across generations, and how beauty resides in everyday objects. The author writes in a very heartfelt and sincere way, and it’s a charming, light read to take with you on a trip to the beach, or to enjoy under a shady tree.” Andrew Kuo B. New York, 1977. Lives and works in New York. Reading: Han Kang, The White Book , 2016 List (12/13/14), 2014-15 Andrew Kuo Rago/Wright/LAMA/Toomey & Co. “Han Kang’s The White Book has been my summer read, in pieces. Her writing fades in and out, like visiting an album or playlist, and her words on death, life, conflict, and peace through the color white feel both heavy and free. Like my favorite artworks, this book is kind of strange and definitively moving, though it has zero jokes, sadly.” Alia Farid B. Kuwait, 1985. Lives and works in Kuwait and Puerto Rico. Reading: Hilda Hilst, With My Dog-Eyes , 1986 “I am reading a couple of books this summer, but the one I will share is With My Dog-Eyes by Hilda Hilst. I don't remember how this book came into my possession or who might have recommended it. But I love the title. “I’ve had it in my studio for a while now and picked it up this summer in search of something different and short, so that I could momentarily tap out of my work. I find Hilda’s irreverent style refreshing, a reminder that whatever appears most normal is most ideological.” Curtis Talwst Santiago B. Edmonton, Canada, 1979. Lives and works in Potsdam, Germany. Reading: Octavia Butler, Parable of the Sower , 1993, and Donella Meadows, Thinking in Systems , 2008 “I’ve been reading Octavia Butler’s Parable of the Sower alongside Donella Meadows’s Thinking in Systems . Meadows gives language to something I keep circling in the studio—feedback loops, thresholds, what gets amplified versus what quietly disappears—close to what’s happening in ‘worlds, worlds, worlds,’ my upcoming show at Contemporary Calgary, where cardboard packaging becomes structure and horns and channels act as apparatuses of transmission and interruption. “Butler’s ‘Earthseed’ philosophy—‘God is Change,’ the idea that change is the only constant, something to be shaped rather than feared—feels close to how I think about working with discarded, unstable materials: not resisting flux but building form out of it. Reading them together this summer feels right for where the show is landing.” Vuslat B. Istanbul, 1971. Lives and works in Istanbul and Los Angeles. Reading: Lewis Hyde, The Gift: Imagination and the Erotic Life of Property , 1983 “The last book I’ve been reading—re-reading, really—is Lewis Hyde’s The Gift: Imagination and the Erotic Life of Property , which has stayed with me in an intimate way. “Hyde reflects on art in relation to giving and receiving, and this resonates with my ongoing exploration of the Turkish concept of emanet, which is entrusted care, responsibility, the invisible threads that connect us. “The book has given form and language to an intuition I have been working with for years. For Hyde, a gift stays alive only as long as it keeps circulating. That has given me a new perspective on my site-specific installation for the 2026 Biennale of Contemporary Ceramics, currently open in Rhodes, Greece. Titled May We Meet In The Silence Of Our Souls (2026), the work consists of ceramic forms shaped through breath—they are small offerings entering a shared space, where they are received, held, and carried forward by those who encounter them. “Since we’re on the subject of books, I would be remiss not to say that my monograph of the same title comes out in America next month from the University of Chicago Press. In May We Meet In The Silence Of Our Souls , Hyde and I enter into a dialogue around these ideas, considering how art can hold and transmit what is entrusted to us. I spent my summer at our family house in Bodrum, on the south coast of Turkey, where three generations of our family come together each summer. It is a time to reconnect with family and friends, share time, and simply enjoy togetherness. To Bodrum, I brought my newly converted tiny house, which serves as my mobile studio. I was also able to continue making art while being surrounded by people I love. For me, it was a beautiful balance between family, friendship, and my practice.” Sarah Blaustein B. San Francisco, 1982. Lives and works in the San Francisco Bay Area. Reading: Stephen King, On Writing: A Memoir of the Craft , 2000 “I’m reading Stephen King’s On Writing: A Memoir of the Craft while I make work for an upcoming group presentation at Untitled Houston for early October with Library Street Collective . “I love the way King describes the process of uncovering one’s story—that’s how I feel I make my own images, by excavating them one studio session at a time. King compares having great, sober sex to the act of writing. He asks why writers can’t stay sane and go completely nuts (creatively) at the same time. That’s how I like to feel in my studio: both ecstatic and entirely clear-sighted.”

title: First Fernando Botero show in London for over a decade to open in October 2026.
summary: Opera Gallery London will open “ Fernando Botero : In Praise of an Amplified World” on October 12th, marking the first solo exhibition of the Colombian artist’s work in London since 2015 Coinciding with the opening of Frieze London , the show continues through November 12th, and brings together paintings, drawings, and sculptures. Works on view will span nearly six decades, from the mid-1960s to the final year of Botero’s life before his passing in 2023. The exhibition, with scenography by designer Cécile Degos, argues against reading Botero’s signature style as caricature, framing volume instead as the artist’s central subject. Rather than simply enlarging his figures and objects, the gallery says, Botero “amplified” them, using shifts in proportion to intensify their physical presence. That approach traces back to a 1957 realization: while painting a mandolin, Botero found that shrinking its rosette made the instrument’s body appear far larger. He later credited that discovery with unlocking his entire visual language. The show also underscores Botero’s lifelong engagement with art history. He worked as a copyist at the Museo del Prado in Madrid in his youth, selling copies of paintings by Diego Velázquez and Francisco Goya to support himself, and the exhibition traces a continuing dialogue in his work with those artists as well as Piero della Francesca and Pablo Picasso . “Fernando Botero created a visual language that is instantly recognisable yet endlessly nuanced,” Opera Gallery founder Gilles Dyan said in a statement. “Bringing together works across more than six decades, this exhibition highlights the remarkable consistency of his artistic vision and the diversity of his achievements.” Botero has seen his market grow substantially since his death. According to the Artnet Price Database , total auction sales of his work reached an all-time high of $53.8 million in 2024, the same year his auction record was set at Christie’s with the $5.1 million sale of his 1979 painting The Musicians . The London show will follow “ Botero in New York ,” an exhibition organized with the Botero family on view at Sotheby’s Breuer building this summer, through September 7th. That show traces how the artist’s years in Greenwich Village in the late 1950s and ’60s helped shape the voluptuous, flattened style that would become known as Boterismo.

title: How to Choose Art for Your Home Office
summary: Ferris Wheel Through Time and Space, 2023 Jesse Meserve TAG The Art Gallery While the days of COVID-19 lockdowns are behind us, remote work has become a fixture of many jobs. As people find themselves working from home, they are paying greater attention to their home offices, brightening and refreshing domestic spots to suit their professional needs and personal taste. “The demand for artworks for home offices has increased, driven by the need to make offices more soulful or simply more entertaining during video calls,” Jane Corkin, founder of Corkin Gallery , told Artsy. “They are looking for works that empower and invigorate. We are seeing bold choices and deeper works that bring a layer of introspection rather than mere decoration.” Whether you’re buying art for the first time or expanding your collection, here are tips from leading galleries and designers on purchasing art that fits into your home working setup seamlessly. Start with the room, not the art Happy Place #9, 2021 Leslie Kerby FROSCH&CO Like any form of purchasing art, deciding what to buy for your workspace requires consideration about where and how you want the art to live. In addition to being heavily used rooms, home offices have to be practical and fit the needs of your job. It’s important to think first about the room and how you use it, assessing the physical constraints—size, layout of furniture, and things like the dominant light source and its direction. North-facing rooms tend to have cooler and more even light, while south-facing rooms are warm and shift through the day. This can change how an artwork appears and create glare, depending on how you frame it. “If a home office gets a lot of natural light, works behind glass—such as photography, drawings, or works on paper—can create reflections that become distracting during the workday, even if they’re barely noticeable in the evening,” said Sarah Sargeant, founder and principal at the New York–based firm Cochineal Design. “It’s worth thinking about the room’s lighting conditions before deciding on framing or medium so the artwork can be enjoyed comfortably throughout the day.” Red Yellow Black White (from Standing People), 2020 Julian Opie Robin Rile Fine Art The overall palette and material feel of the room is also important to consider. A dark space with warm surfaces like leather will need different artworks than a minimal setup with white walls. While your workspace may have specific needs, it’s still a part of your home. “I think an office should feel like a natural extension of the rest of the home, rather than a space with an entirely different look and feel,” Sargeant added. “I always prefer to propose artwork that complements a home's broader collection and design story. That said, every client is different.” What artworks tend to work for home offices, and why Still In The Game , 2022 Yoon Hyup APC Gallery Yo Ho Ho , 2008 Todd James aous Once you’ve understood the requirements of your space, you can start to think about what will work for your home office. For many people, the wall behind a desk is the best place to hang artwork. Some might find it better to have a single piece proportioned to their room and furniture, but what works for one person might not be best for another. In his own home office, Mohamed Benhadj, director and curator of Al-Tiba9 Gallery , has a variety of pieces, including a sculpture, photograph, and a neon installation. “I enjoy living with different materials and different artistic languages throughout the day,” he said. “The neon wall installation offers me a new atmosphere at night and keeps me inspired. I always encourage collectors to be creative in their choices and not limit themselves to a single artwork or a single medium.” Indeed, when you spend hours in the same room, it’s important to think about how you’d like to feel in the morning as well as after a long day of work. You may have to be flexible as you start to live with your artwork. “We’ve worked with collectors who relocate works from living and dining rooms into their home offices because they realize those are the pieces they want to spend the most time with,” said Emily Siekkinen, director of Octavia Art Gallery . In terms of cost, works on paper, prints , and photography can be more accessible and are easier to hang and move around as you decide on an arrangement. “A home office is a smaller and more intimate space, and prints tend to work beautifully at that scale—they don’t overwhelm the room the way a large unique painting might, and they let you live with a serious artist’s work without needing museum-sized walls,” said Elisabetta Setzu, senior director of print specialist Gemini G.E.L . “There’s also something appropriate about prints for a workspace: They represent the artist’s hand and process in a very direct way.” “We’re seeing strong interest in artists whose prints reward close, sustained looking,” added Setzu. “ Vija Celmins ’s drypoints, Richard Tuttle ’s hand-drawn works, and Ed Ruscha ’s word-based prints all come up often for home offices specifically, since they're contemplative rather than purely decorative.” Size, placement, and the video call factor My Desktop 我的書桌, 2018 Guanyu Xu Galerie du Monde Ultimately, the artwork you choose needs to suit your profession. If your office blurs the public-private boundary and you have visitors or are often on video calls, you might have to be more deliberate about what you hang on your walls. “A therapist, for instance, may want to create a space that feels welcoming, calming, and conducive to vulnerability,” Rachel Vincent-Clarke, director of Galerie Robertson Arès , said. “An entrepreneur might choose works that embody the values, creativity, or visual identity of their business.” Dealers also suggest artwork that rewards slow viewing, given the amount of time you will spend with it. “One of our collectors shared a photograph of a recent acquisition from our gallery, newly installed in her home office: a subtly hued embroidery on raw canvas by Montreal-based textile artist Cyndie Belhumeur ,” Vincent-Clarke added. “The work explores our relationship with the digital world, reflecting on the overwhelming flow of information that surrounds us while reminding us of our capacity to pause, step back, and recalibrate. I think that’s a particularly resonant theme for a home office.” Practically speaking for video callers, your camera position should be considered when judging where to hang something behind you. If a work is too large, it might not translate well through a screen. Common mistakes Westie at Work, 2026 Scott Reeder Saenger Galería While keeping these more practical tips in mind can help you choose the best artwork for your home office, there are additional caveats. People can spend hours on end in their workspace, so dealers caution against buying something you think will look good, but isn’t what you really want. “Only purchase artwork that you’ll want to live with, not just look at occasionally,” said Siekkinen. “A home office is one of the few places where you engage with the same artwork every day, so choosing something that will continue to hold your interest is important.” Still, a piece should be interesting without being diverting. An eye-catching work could be a good conversation starter or could become a distraction. People who give group presentations might find it challenging to keep their audience’s attention. Moreover, what’s hanging on the walls might become a distraction to you. “An artwork that makes you feel motivated to work is very different from one that constantly makes you dream about going on holiday or taking a day off,” noted Benhadj.

title: Black Mid-Century Artist Felrath Hines Is Finally Getting His Due for His Luminous Abstractions
summary: He was a member of the Spiral Group , the pioneering collective of African American artists in the 1960s, and an artistic peer to Romare Bearden and Emma Amos . Georgia O’Keeffe so admired his talents that she hired him as a personal conservator to her paintings. But, today, artist Felrath Hines , who died in 1993, is largely unknown—even in the art world. “Hines was strongly devoted to abstraction and pursued it with a very independent and persistent attitude,” said Andrew Schoelkopf, the owner and founder of New York’s Schoelkopf Gallery . Right now, the gallery is presenting an intimate showcase of Hines’s works, on view through August 21st. The exhibition includes five key paintings by the artist from the 1950s and ’60s, decades when he produced evocative abstractions painted in bold but sensuous brushstrokes. The exhibition is part of the gallery’s ongoing effort to shine new light on Hines’s career, and builds on a 2022 solo presentation of his work at ADAA: The Art Show in New York. The jewel of this exhibition is The Bush from 1962, a gestural abstraction painted in foggy passages of greens, purples, and grays, like a landscape seen in the distance of a misty shore. The work is emblematic of Hines’s best paintings of the 1960s. “You can see how his brushwork is the work of an adept painter. It’s rich and layered, which creates a certain luminosity in the surface. I also find his sense of color to be tremendously skillful and alluring,” said Schoelkopf. Bouquet, 1957 Felrath Hines Schoelkopf Gallery Landscape, 1953 Felrath Hines Schoelkopf Gallery The gallery first became interested in Hines’s works while researching the Spiral Group , a collective of African American artists who explored the role of art in relation to society and the Civil Rights Movement. “As a member of the Spiral Group, he was a prominent figure in the New York City art world and the Black creative scene of the time,” added Schoelkopf. Still, unlike other Black artists of the era , such as Bearden or Jacob Lawrence , Hines’s story has remained largely untold. Born Samuel Felrath Hines Jr. in Indianapolis in 1913, the artist had his first forays into art as a teenager, after receiving a scholarship for classes at the John Herron School of Art Saturday School. Following high school, he worked as a firefighter, and as a railway waiter, earning money to support classes at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago . By 1946, he had moved to New York where he studied with the Russian-born American painter Nahum Tschacbasov , while also taking classes at New York University and Pratt. By 1951, Hines had started working at a frame shop in the city. His skill as a painter and his knowledge of framing eventually led him into a career as a conservator at New York’s Fine Arts Conservation Laboratories. His career as a conservator and his practice as an artist were side by side for most of his life. Over the years, he took major positions at the Museum of Modern Art , the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden , and the Smithsonian’s National Portrait Gallery . Early in his conservator career, he helped conserve one of Claude Monet ’s “Water Lilies” paintings for MoMA, an experience that informed his own luminous palette and layered approach to abstraction (the influence is evident in a work like The Bush ). Later, Georgia O’Keeffe would bring on Hines to lead the conservation of her personal collection, as well as the care of her works in private and museum collections during the 1970s. Distant View, 1962 Felrath Hines Schoelkopf Gallery Sea Shell, 1962 Felrath Hines Schoelkopf Gallery Hines’s painting style continued to evolve. His gestural abstractions, now on view at Schoelkopf Gallery, later gave way to geometric abstractions influenced by De Stijl and Piet Mondrian . While Hines was an active participant in the Spiral Group, he always maintained a very individualized artistic vision. “Despite his predilection for looking at art in exhibits and galleries, he never painted with other artists,” wrote historian Rachel Berenson Perry in her defining monograph of the artist, The Life and Art of Felrath Hines: From Dark to Light. The artist wasn’t one to seek the limelight, either. “He was a regular social presence in the New York art world, especially in Black creative circles, but he didn’t like to draw attention to himself,” said Schoelkopf. Throughout his career, Hines also resisted being classified primarily as a Black artist and believed his work, and abstraction, were universal languages in their expression and reach. As such, he turned down invitations to exhibit in shows focused on the work of Black artists alone, including the major exhibition “Contemporary Black Artists in America” at the Whitney Museum of American Art in 1971. These decisions may have contributed to his relative obscurity. His career as a conservator, at times, detracted from his art practice, too. “He was very dedicated to his work, but he went through long periods of time where his ‘day job’ as a conservator prevented him from spending any time working on his personal creative practice,” said Schoelkopf. A 1979 article described Hines as having “two careers: executing his own art and repairing the art of others.” In 1984, he retired as the chief conservator of the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden, and devoted the last years of his life entirely to painting, creating some of the most significant works of geometric abstraction in his career. He continued to believe in the power of art, despite never reaching widespread fame. In 1983, he said in an interview, “In my view, an artist’s work is to rearrange everyday phenomena so as to enlarge our perception of who we are and what goes on about us.” Today, Hines’s reputation is steadily growing (Schoelkopf Gallery has placed his works with institutions including the Cincinnati Art Museum). Schoelkopf says that with Hines one can’t help but notice “how razor-thin the margin is between the type of success Georgia O’Keeffe had” and that of “an artist as well educated, well trained, intelligent, and important as Felrath Hines.” The art world, he thinks, may soon be catching up.

title: Prado Museum digitally transforms masterpieces by Velázquez, Rubens, and others ahead of August solar eclipse.
summary: The Museo Nacional del Prado in Madrid has released an AI-assisted video, titled “ The Prado by the Light of the Eclipse ,” that digitally alters 11 paintings in its collection to show how their scenes might look under the dimming light of a solar eclipse. The one-minute piece, soundtracked by “Summer” from Vivaldi’s The Four Seasons , is timed to Spain’s total solar eclipse on Wednesday, August 12th. The eclipse—which will also pass over parts of the Northern Hemisphere—will be the first to cross Spain in more than a century, with totality expected to last under two minutes. The video opens with Diego Velázquez ’s Las Meninas (1656) swept into shadow, and goes on to darken Francisco Goya ’s El Quitasol (1777) and La pradera de San Isidro (1788), Peter Paul Rubens and Jan Brueghel the Elder’s La Vista (1617), and Albrecht Dürer ’s self-portrait, among other works by José de Ribera , Corrado Giaquinto , Claude Lorrain , José Casado del Alisal, and Carlos de Haes. In a statement, the Prado described Las Meninas ’s spatial complexity as owing partly to “the multiplication of the light sources,” while El Quitasol points to Goya’s “mastery at painting light and shadows,” the same qualities the new video sets out to manipulate. The project was produced by the Madrid studio AMB Piensa, which combined AI video-generation tools with traditional animation and manual review. According to the museum, the technology was used to simulate the eclipse’s gradual darkening, along with shifting shadows and reflections across each painting’s figures, landscapes, and architecture. Every sequence was checked and adjusted by hand to preserve the works’ original composition and technique. The Prado has also framed the effort as a tool for cultural outreach, aimed particularly at audiences who don’t typically visit museums. This week’s eclipse is the first of three (two total, one partial) forecast to cross Spain and Portugal between now and January 2028, drawing tourists to the Iberian Peninsula for what astronomers describe as a rare run of visibility. It also continues a long tradition of art responding to eclipses. In 1918, the American painter Howard Russell Butler was commissioned by the U.S. Naval Observatory to capture an eclipse on canvas , working from mere seconds of direct observation. Eclipses have also featured in Christian iconography for centuries, tied by some biblical interpretations to the crucifixion. The Prado’s works span several Old Masters traditions, from Velázquez’s Spanish Golden Age portraiture to Rubens’s Flemish Baroque and Dürer’s Northern Renaissance printmaking. The museum’s eclipse video underscores how radically shifting light can transform even familiar paintings.

title: Indian Gallerist Sundaram Tagore Credits Friendships for His International Success
